newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices confirm market's bullish sentiment.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices confirm market's bullish sentiment.

text.p: World oil prices ignored bearish U.S. stock data and Iraq's looming crude exports and notched up further gains on Wednesday in confirmation of bullish market sentiment, brokers said.

World benchmark crude Brent Blend for January delivery rose to an intra-day high of $23.85 a barrel, a gain of eight cents, before easing back to $23.77 a barrel at 1723 GMT, unchanged on Tuesday's close.
The earlier rise coincided with a stronger performance by New York's light crude West Texas Intermediate (WTI) contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX).
Brokers said this proved that even bearish data released on Tuesday and Wednesday in the United States showing a rise in crude and heating oil inventories failed to dent the market.

NYMEX futures opened lower after the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) released its weekly stock figures on Wednesday but later recovered. The EIA data showed a build in crude stocks and an increase in stocks of distillates, which include heating oil.
"(NYMEX) crude broke through $25 and we just went up," a broker said. "This market is bullish whatever the DOE (Department of Energy) says. There isn't enough to go around."
The weekly U.S. stock data is keenly watched by the market for direction on the energy needs of the world's largest consumer.
But with Iraqi crude still out of the market, analysts say the fundamentals of tight supply have determined market direction and kept a sold floor under prices.

"Think of the market as a car. Now envision the inventory levels as shock absorbers. The problem we face is that every time we hit a bump or pothole (supply news), the effect is magnified, not dampened by our shock absorbers," said Charles Gray, first vice-president of investments at Prudential Bache Securities in London.
He was referring to the market's vulnerability to a supply crunch without the comfort cushion of stocks, which remain at historically low levels despite weekly blips up or down.

Gray said in a market report that any disruptions to supply, such as the closure of Mexican ports earlier this week because of storms or strikes at refineries in France, were enough to prompt higher prices.
Analysts say the tight supply scenario is why the possible resumption of Iraqi crude oil exports during a winter market is unlikely to lead to a sell-off.

They point out that the Organisation of Exporting Countries (OPEC) is producing nearly one million barrels per day (bpd) above its quota of 25.03 million bpd without Iraq and the market is absorbing every barrel without a negative impact on prices.

Iraqi oil has been under a U.N. embargo since the August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Baghdad is preparing to export its first crude in six years under the partial oil sales agreement with the United Nations to buy humanitarian goods.
"The Mexican port closures (now resolved) and the Elf strikes (resolvable) gave us a short burst in the face of potential mid-month Iraqi oil flows," Gray said.
